title: Period-dependent suppression of Fourier peaks for topography images: Analysis of periodicity of triple-step arrays on vicinal Si(h h m) surfaces
authors: A. Yu. Aladyshkin, A. N. Chaika, V. N. Semenov, A. S. Aladyshkina, A. M. Ionov, S. I. Bozhko
abstract: Reliable determination of the periodicity of multiatomic steps on high-Miller-index vicinal surfaces is often complicated by (i) the presence of relatively narrow terraces tilted at large angles relative to the scanning plane, and (ii) unavoidable distortions in the lateral direction resulting from creep and improper calibration of a piezo scanner. We argue that the period of the triple-step arrays on vicinal Si(5\,5\,6) and Si(5 5 7) single-crystal wafers can be determined from raw scanning tunneling microscopy data, without preliminary corrections, with precision approaching the interatomic distance. We demonstrate that the intensity of the Fourier peaks of the differential maps, derived from raw topography images by the difference-of-Gaussians approach, strongly depends on the period of the ordered triple-step arrays. This suppression of the ninth Fourier peak indicates that the regular array of triple steps has a period of $18b=5.99$ nm in projection onto the Si(1 1 1) terrace plane, where $b=0.333$ nm is the distance between atomic rows of the $1\times 1$ lattice in the $[\bar{1}\,\bar{1}\,2]$ direction. This means that the nominally (5\,5\,7)-oriented Si wafers may correspond locally to the Si(8 8 11) orientation. The method can be applied to the precise analysis of other vicinal surfaces with narrow and wide terraces containing an integer number of Si(1 1 1)$7\times 7$ unit cells.
summary: This paper presents a novel method for determining the periodicity of atomic step arrays on vicinal silicon surfaces using raw Scanning Tunneling Microscopy data. By applying Difference-of-Gaussians filtering and analyzing the Fourier transform's characteristic peak suppression, the authors achieved high precision in measuring the step period. This technique allows for accurate characterization of surface crystallography even when traditional measurement methods fail due to instrumental artifacts.
main_problem: The reliable determination of periodicity for multiatomic steps on high-Miller-index vicinal Si surfaces is difficult due to surface tilt, narrow terraces, and instrumental distortions.
main_result: By analyzing the Fourier transform of differential maps derived from raw STM topography data, the authors determined a precise period of 5.99 nm for triple-step arrays, suggesting a local $	ext{Si}(8 8 11)$ orientation on nominally $(5 5 7)$-oriented wafers.
method: The analysis uses Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) data processed via the Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) approach to generate differential maps. Periodicity is extracted by analyzing the period-dependent suppression of specific Fourier peaks in the FFT pattern.
model_or_system: The physical system is vicinal single-crystal silicon wafers ($	ext{Si}(h h m)$), specifically focusing on periodic triple-step staircases formed on $	ext{Si}(5 5 7)$. The analysis models the adatom concentration function averaged over the surface.
key_observables: The intensity and pattern of Fourier peaks (specifically, the suppression of specific $m$-th order peaks) in the differential map's FFT.
important_parameters: Periodicity ($L$), interatomic distance ($b=0.333$ nm), and the number of $	ext{Si}(1 1 1)$ unit cells involved in the structure (e.g., $7 	imes 7$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the periodic structures are commensurable with the underlying crystal lattice, allowing for Fourier analysis to reveal periodicity-dependent suppression effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the DoG processing of topography images and show model calculations where the expected period ($L=16b, 17b, 18b$) dictates which specific Fourier peaks are suppressed in the resulting FFT pattern.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the difficulty of traditional measurements on stepped surfaces, introduces the DoG processing technique to mitigate artifacts, and then uses theoretical modeling (based on adatom concentration) combined with experimental observation of peak suppression to derive the precise local surface orientation and periodicity.
why_interesting: While not directly quantum information theory, this work represents a highly advanced application of signal processing (Fourier analysis) to characterize nanoscale physical structures, which shares mathematical rigor with analyzing correlation functions in condensed matter systems.
